claim: When a jailbreak attack succeeds against a safety-aligned LLM, the model's safety-relevant internal representations are not eliminated — they are bypassed. The attack selectively suppresses a small subset of attention heads, and suppressing that subset is by itself enough to turn a refusal into a compliance, while other heads go on representing the harmful content even as the attack succeeds. Because those representations persist, they can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, with no additional training, at a quality competitive with dedicated safety models.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaim "What happens to a safety-aligned LLM’s safety-relevant internal representations when a jailbreak attack succeeds?" and the paired subclaims about elimination vs bypass, run a mechanistic comparison on a public safety-aligned open-weight model such as Llama-2-Chat, Llama-3-Instruct, or Qwen2.5-Instruct using harmful/refusal benchmarks from HuggingFace or JailbreakBench plus benign controls from Anthropic HH-RLHF or WildChat. First, collect three prompt conditions for the same harmful intent: direct harmful request that is refused, jailbreak-wrapped harmful request that is complied with, and benign request. Record layerwise residual-stream activations and attention-head outputs for all conditions. Then train simple linear probes only on the refused-harmful vs benign contrast at each layer/head family, and test those probes zero-shot on jailbreak-successful harmful prompts. If probes trained to detect harmful intent in the refused condition still score jailbreaked harmful inputs as harmful at high AUROC, while the model behavior changes from refusal to compliance, that supports bypass rather than elimination. If probe scores collapse on jailbreaked harmful inputs toward benign levels, that supports elimination or severe corruption of safety-relevant representations. A useful extension is representational similarity analysis or CCA between refused-harmful and jailbreak-harmful internal states after controlling for lexical overlap; persistent similarity in harm-related directions despite different outputs would strengthen the bypass interpretation. This experiment could be made less necessary if there were already public mechanistic traces showing layerwise harmful-intent probes remain active during successful jailbreaks across multiple models and attack families.

To address subclaim "What does the jailbreak attack selectively suppress?" identify whether successful jailbreaks consistently reduce activity in a small subset of attention heads. Using the same public models and prompt sets, compute per-head metrics under refused harmful prompts versus matched successful jailbreak prompts: attention output norm, direct logit attribution to refusal tokens, causal effect from head ablation, and activation patching score. Rank heads by the drop in these metrics during jailbreak success, and test whether the same small set recurs across prompts, attack templates, and models. To avoid confounding from token-position differences, compare within matched prompt pairs and use token-aligned windows near the model’s decision to refuse or comply. If a compact subset of heads shows large, reproducible suppression specifically when jailbreaks succeed, that supports the claim of selective suppression. If suppression is diffuse across many heads or concentrated in MLPs or residual-stream directions instead, the subclaim is weakened or revised. If no stable suppressed subset appears across attacks, then the mechanism may be attack-specific rather than general. This experiment would be partly unnecessary if prior evidence already provided robust, cross-model causal maps of refusal-related heads and showed jailbreaks consistently downregulate exactly those heads.

To address subclaim "Is suppressing a small subset of attention heads enough to turn a refusal into compliance?" perform direct causal interventions on the candidate suppressed heads found in the previous experiment. On harmful prompts that the aligned model normally refuses, ablate, zero, mean-replace, or scale down only the identified heads during generation, leaving the rest of the network unchanged. Measure the change in refusal rate, harmful compliance rate, and generation quality on benign prompts. Include controls that suppress an equal number of randomly selected heads, the next-best-ranked heads, and matched-norm heads. If suppressing just the candidate subset reliably converts refusals into harmful compliance far more often than control head sets, that strongly supports sufficiency. If many larger head sets or random sets cause similar compliance, then the claim that a small specific subset is sufficient is weakened. If suppression merely degrades coherence without increasing harmful compliance, then those heads may correlate with refusal rather than cause it. This experiment becomes less necessary if existing intervention studies already show that ablating a compact refusal-head circuit reproducibly flips outputs from refusal to compliance with minimal side effects.

To address subclaim "Do other attention heads continue representing harmful content even when the jailbreak attack succeeds?" test whether heads outside the suppressed subset still encode harmfulness during successful jailbreaks. Build head-level or layer-level readouts from the non-suppressed components only, again trained on refused-harmful vs benign prompts or using unsupervised directions such as mean-difference vectors between harmful and benign conditions. Evaluate these readouts on successful jailbreak prompts, and perform causal tracing or activation patching to confirm that information about harmful intent is localized in non-suppressed heads during those runs. One can also decode structured attributes of the harmful request, such as weapon/drug/self-harm category from public moderation datasets like OpenAI Moderation-style public replicas on HuggingFace, BeaverTails, ToxicChat, or WildGuardMix, using only activations from non-suppressed heads. If non-suppressed heads retain strong decodable harmfulness and category information during jailbreak success, this supports the persistence claim. If harmful information becomes largely undecodable outside the suppressed heads, then bypass is less plausible and stronger representational collapse is indicated. This experiment could be shortened if previous analyses already demonstrated that harm-relevant information remains linearly decodable from residual or head activations after the refusal circuit is disabled.

To address subclaim "Can the persistent representations be read out directly as a harmful-input detector?" and "Does using these representations as a harmful-input detector require additional training?" evaluate training-free detectors built from internal representations on public harmfulness datasets such as BeaverTails, ToxicChat, WildGuardMix, JailbreakBench, and benign instruction datasets from Alpaca or UltraChat. Construct zero-training scores using methods like cosine similarity to a harm direction estimated from a small fixed public prompt set, nearest-neighbor scoring from a frozen bank of harmful vs benign exemplars, logit-lens scoring onto refusal-related vocabulary, or direct use of a previously identified residual direction without fitting new classifier weights on the evaluation data. Critically, separate any calibration prompts from test datasets and report AUROC, AUPRC, calibration, and robustness to paraphrase and jailbreak wrappers. If these no-additional-training detectors achieve strong discrimination on held-out harmful inputs, especially successful jailbreak prompts, the claim is supported. If acceptable detection requires fitting a learned probe or substantial labeled calibration, the no-additional-training subclaim is weakened. If performance is brittle across domains, the direct-readout idea may still hold only narrowly. This experiment would be less necessary if a public benchmark already showed frozen internal-direction scores transfer well across multiple harmfulness datasets without any fitted classifier.

To address subclaim "How does the quality of this harmful-input detector compare with dedicated safety models?" benchmark the best training-free internal detector against public safety classifiers and moderation models on the same held-out datasets and jailbreak sets. Candidate baselines should include open models such as Llama Guard, WildGuard, Aegis, ShieldGemma, or other public moderation checkpoints available on HuggingFace, plus simple lexical baselines. Evaluate standard metrics overall and by slice: direct harmful prompts, successful jailbreak prompts, benign prompts containing harmful words in non-actionable contexts, multilingual subsets if available, and adversarial paraphrases. Also compare compute cost and latency, since an internal detector may be cheaper if it reuses the base model’s activations. If the internal detector matches or exceeds dedicated safety models on AUROC/AUPRC and maintains robustness on jailbreak-success cases, the competitiveness claim is supported. If it trails substantially except on narrow slices, then the claim should be narrowed. If it only works on the same model it is extracted from while safety models transfer better across models and domains, that is an important limitation. This experiment could be made less necessary if there were already a public head-to-head benchmark showing frozen-representation detectors are competitive with current open moderation models across standard harmfulness and jailbreak evaluations.
reference_experiments: Before identifying any component, test the premise that attacks bypass rather than erase safety representations. On inputs where a jailbreak succeeded, measure activation of the refusal direction across all layers and components (attention heads and MLPs) and compare against the same requests unattacked. If a successful attack flattens refusal activation everywhere, attacks do break safety representations and everything downstream is dead. The authors find mid layers still maintain substantial refusal activation under successful attack, particularly in the layers previously identified as most safety-relevant.

Construct the paired evaluation set the whole analysis depends on. Sample benign prompts from Alpaca, collect harmful behaviours from published harmful-behaviour datasets, generate attack variants with GCG, AutoDAN, many-shot jailbreaking and PAIR, and retain only pairs where the unattacked request is refused and the attacked version succeeds. Within-pair comparison is what separates the attack's effect from differences between requests. The authors obtain 378 (Llama-2-7B-Chat) and 176 (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) usable pairs from roughly 10,000 attack samples, a 2-3% yield that caps the study's statistical power.

Build and calibrate the component-scoring instrument. Extract the refusal direction by difference-in-means and select the optimal layer, project it into each attention head's output space to score that head's contribution to the refusal signal, and classify heads by distribution overlap between conditions using two-stage filtering. Then verify the classification is not an artifact of the cut point by sweeping the threshold and the KDE bandwidth. The authors use thresholds of 0.5, find stability across 0.4-0.6, and obtain 21 ACHs and 17 SAHs for Llama-3 (416 heads analysed) and 20 ACHs and 19 SAHs for Llama-2 (480 analysed), with ACHs concentrated in layers 0-3 and SAHs in layers 5-12.

Test causally whether suppressing the identified heads is sufficient to cause attack success. On harmful inputs the model normally refuses (baseline ASR about 0%), inject a negative refusal-direction feature into ACH outputs, progressively increase the number of intervened heads, and measure attack success rate — with a matched random-head intervention as control, 10 seeds and 95% confidence intervals. Without the random-head arm the effect cannot be attributed to those heads rather than to perturbing that many heads at all. The authors report ACH intervention driving ASR to 99.5% (Llama-3) and 83.7% (Llama-2), reaching 95.0% and 81.6% at just 8 heads, against 4.0% +/- 3.7 and 10.2% +/- 11.6 for random heads.

Test whether the other head type is a real source of the persistent signal. Apply the same suppression to SAHs, this time on attack inputs, and measure the change in mid-layer activation strength using mean absolute activation across mid-layer heads. The authors report Llama-2 falling from 0.222 to 0.181 (18%) and Llama-3 from 0.0062 to 0.0053 (14%), against a reference of 0.397 and 0.0086 under unattacked harmful inputs.

Discriminate the mechanistic account from the rival explanation that the two head types simply differ in sensitivity to harmful content. Using the linearity of attention, attribute each head's activation to individual input tokens, separate the contribution of the original harmful-request tokens from that of the attack-template tokens, and compare the two head types on each. The account holds only if the types are indistinguishable on the harmful request itself and separate sharply on the attack template. The authors report medians within +/-0.15 on harmful tokens, against roughly -1.5 for ACHs and +1.5 for SAHs on attack-template tokens.

Validate externally that the persistent signal generalises and is useful. Build a training-free detector that reads standardised activations at discriminative positions via top-m aggregation and thresholds the score, then evaluate Macro-F1 on ten safety-eval benchmarks across six models from three architecture families, against both the model's own refusal behaviour and trained guard models. If the readout does not transfer, the phenomenon is a property of the two models analysed. The authors report Gemma-2B improving from 0.470 to 0.853 and Qwen-7B from 0.506 to 0.860 overall, SALAD-Bench from 0.270 to 0.976, and Llama-3-8B reaching 0.888 weighted average against WildGuard 0.880 and LlamaGuard3/4 at 0.599/0.666.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A within-request, layer- and component-resolved comparison that can distinguish retained safety-relevant representations from their disappearance during a successful attack.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed comparison records layerwise residual and head outputs for refused and successfully jailbreaked versions of the same harmful intent, and tests a harm probe trained only before the attack on the jailbreak condition. The simultaneous persistence of the readout and change in behavior directly tests bypass versus representational loss; the recorded layerwise activations also permit the direct comparison rather than relying only on output behavior.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A paired evaluation corpus containing the same harmful intents in a refused baseline condition and a successful jailbreak condition, with enough attack diversity to make within-pair comparisons informative.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed studies use matched harmful prompts with direct refusals and successful jailbreak wrappers, and explicitly call for within-pair comparisons across prompt sets and attack templates. This supplies the essential control that separates attack effects from differences in the underlying harmful requests; the particular source datasets and attack algorithms are not binding in the claim.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A reproducible quantitative procedure for ranking attention heads by attack-related change in refusal-relevant activity and identifying a compact, stable suppressed group rather than an arbitrary set of heads.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed head analysis evaluates several independent per-head signals, ranks heads by the change between matched refused and successful-jailbreak conditions, and tests recurrence across prompts, attack templates, and models. The causal intervention and comparison with multiple matched control head sets then provide an additional check that the selected compact group is meaningful rather than merely a ranking artifact.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A controlled causal intervention showing that suppressing the identified compact head group, rather than perturbing an equal number of arbitrary heads, is sufficient to convert refusal into harmful compliance.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed intervention directly ablates, zeros, replaces, or scales down only the candidate heads during generation and measures refusal and harmful-compliance rates. Random, next-best, and matched-norm head controls, together with benign-prompt quality checks, discriminate a specific refusal flip from generic network damage.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Evidence that heads outside the selectively suppressed group still carry decodable and functionally relevant harmful-content information during successful jailbreaks.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed experiment builds readouts using only non-suppressed heads and evaluates them on successful jailbreaks, with optional causal tracing or activation patching to test localization. Persistent harmfulness or category information under that restricted readout, especially with a causal localization check, establishes the same persistence property by a different route than measuring a particular aggregate activation norm.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Token-level attribution that separates original harmful-request information from attack-wrapper information and compares the two head populations, ruling out mere differential sensitivity to harmful content.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed experiments use matched prompts, lexical-overlap controls, attack-template variation, and harmful-category decoding, so they bear on whether the effect is specific to jailbreak context. However, they do not decompose each head's activation into contributions from the original harmful-request tokens versus the attack-template tokens and compare the two head groups on those separate contributions.
reasoning_chain: The reference experiment distinguishes the proposed specialization mechanism from the rival explanation that the head groups merely have different sensitivity to harmful content.

Proposed 0 controls some representational confounds and proposed 1 varies attack templates in matched comparisons, while proposed 3 tests whether harmful information remains decodable outside the candidate suppressed heads.
None of the proposed experiments performs the decisive token-level source attribution or directly compares the two head groups on harmful-request tokens and wrapper tokens.
Consequently, a stable suppressed subset and persistent decodability could still be explained by differential sensitivity to wrapper/context tokens rather than the claimed specialization.
A team running the proposed set would fail to learn whether the head-type contrast survives that harmful-content-versus-attack-template sensitivity confound.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An external held-out evaluation of a training-free internal readout across varied harmfulness domains and model contexts, accompanied by head-to-head comparison with dedicated safety detectors.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed detector evaluation uses separated calibration and test data, multiple harmfulness and jailbreak domains, robustness slices, and metrics such as AUROC and AUPRC. The companion benchmark compares the best frozen internal readout with several dedicated moderation checkpoints and lexical baselines on the same held-out cases, directly testing both no-additional-training use and competitive quality.

sufficiency_reasoning: Taken together, the proposed set tests the full contractual claim: matched refused-versus-successful-jailbreak behavior, persistence of safety-relevant information, identification of a compact suppressed head group, causal sufficiency with specific controls, persistence in other heads, and a training-free external detector benchmarked against dedicated safety models. runs.sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set directly covers the contract's central claims: persistence of harmful/safety-relevant representations during successful jailbreaks, selective concentration in a compact head subset, causal conversion of refusal to compliance, retention of harmful information in other heads, and a training-free detector benchmarked against dedicated safety models. The remaining gap is mechanistic attribution: without separating original harmful-request tokens from jailbreak-wrapper tokens, the team could establish the behavioral and representational pattern while leaving one important rival explanation unresolved.

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: Taken together, the proposed set tests persistence versus collapse, identifies a compact selectively affected head subset, intervenes on that subset with specificity controls, checks retained harmful information in other heads, constructs a detector without fitting a new evaluation-data classifier, and compares it with dedicated safety models. The token-level mechanistic attribution from the reference is not fully reproduced, but it is ancillary to the stated claim: the proposed causal and representational experiments can still establish bypass, selective suppression, persistence, and detector competitiveness. The remaining ambiguity concerns the finer explanation of why the two head types differ, not whether the main claim is supported.
